extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics instructors and assessment designers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for assessing undergraduate mathematics learning, designing tests, classroom assessment techniques (CATs), colloquium/student-presentation evaluation, and using interactive e-mail/automated portfolios for feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public attendance tracking with incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: At the front of the room we hang a poster-sized attendance sheet for the entire semester with the heading “Colloquium Attendance Prize.” (We do give a small prize at the end of the year to the student who attends the most talks.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publicly posted attendance sheet encourages students to be responsible about coming to talks; the small prize is a reasonable cover cost. Also, relax strict frequency requirements (e.g., require a number of talks per semester rather than one each week) to increase reliability and fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of faculty evaluation after student talks
rubrics_metrics.description: Faculty used to evaluate a talk immediately afterwards, leaving students to chat over tea. Now we delay our meeting a bit, talking with students about the colloquium or other matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delaying the verdict gives a relaxed time to interact (over cookies and soda), benefits both students and faculty, and reduces the chance that students will leave before receiving feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardized timetable for preparing talks
rubrics_metrics.description: We now have, to some extent, standardized the timetable under which talks are prepared, so students know, for example, that they have to pick an advisor at least four weeks before the talk and give at least one practice talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear deadlines and expectations (advisor selection four weeks prior, mandatory practice talk) reduce student confusion arising from wide variations in faculty advising styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing advising workload among faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than set specific limits on the number of talks one can advise, we prefer to remind ourselves annually that an imbalance may occur, and then keep an eye on each other and especially on nontenured colleagues, encouraging them to say no if they feel overburdened advising talks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor distribution of advising requests, support junior faculty in declining excess advising, and avoid rigid quotas while being attentive to workload equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project group sizing for summer research (SMALL Project format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participants now work with only one faculty member in one group of three students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing groups from two groups of four–five students to one group of three with a single faculty mentor increases focus, productivity, and student satisfaction; be aware of the small risk that a student might not find their single group engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of Senior Colloquium presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Seniors gain independence, poise, and confidence even as they learn a healthy respect for the effort required to prepare a good presentation. We think the Senior Colloquium is one of the best aspects of our major.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these benefits, consider adding presentation components to advanced courses to both enhance those courses and prepare students for the Senior Colloquium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Classroom Assessment Techniques (CATs) as formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: CATs are ways to find out whether students understand a concept, and what difficulties they are having with it, before they fail the test on it. Traditional assessment is summative; CATs are formative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CATs to diagnose misunderstandings early so students can learn and instructors can adjust teaching; many CATs also help students learn through participation in the assessment itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design tests to assess understanding not just computations
rubrics_metrics.description: For students to believe that we expect them to understand the ideas, not just be able to do computations, our tests must reflect this expectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct test items that require conceptual thinking, interpretation, explanation, and application, not merely routine computations; communicate these expectations to students before the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align test design with course goals (skill-building vs concept-development)
rubrics_metrics.description: We see some of our entry-level courses primarily as skill-building courses, others as concept-development courses. Changes in course goals have resulted in changes in instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the course emphasizes skills or concepts (or both) and design assessments accordingly; discuss what each course is about, what is needed for subsequent courses, and what can really be measured (especially when using common finals or technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing skills: require mental demonstration and appropriate timing
rubrics_metrics.description: When we do want to evaluate mathematical skills, we ask directly for those things we think are best done mentally. We try to be careful about time requirements as we want to assess skill not speed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include items that require students to show they can do the skill (e.g., 'Use a 3×3 system to demonstrate that you know and can apply Cramer's rule'), and design time limits that assess skill rather than penalize slower processing unrelated to mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation tasks for conceptual assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation tasks are one way to open a window into student understanding. Often a student can identify or classify mathematical objects of a certain type, but cannot create an object with specified characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use problems that require students to construct examples meeting detailed constraints (e.g., 'Create a polynomial of fifth degree...'; 'Create a function continuous on [–5,5] whose derivative is positive on [–5,3) and negative on (3,5]'). These reveal deeper understanding than recognition tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse questions to probe learning transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing the type of question on which the student has been practicing is a good way to investigate whether students are really learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask students to produce a function given its graph, or to explain why a given graph cannot be of a specified type (e.g., 'Why can the graph given not be the graph of a fourth degree polynomial function?') to test flexible application of skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition between representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Test items that require connecting representations or moving from one to another can strengthen these skills as well as reveal gaps in understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require students to move among verbal, symbolic, numeric, graphical representations (e.g., 'What happens to an ellipse when its foci are pushed together? Confirm using a symbolic representation'), and include tasks matching columns of f, f', f'' values to reinforce representation fluency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess understanding in the presence of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: When technology is used regularly to handle routine computations, there is a possibility that intuition and a 'feel' for the concept is being slighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design items that technology cannot fully handle or that require students to use technology to confirm intuition but not replace it (e.g., ask which function has larger average rate of change and require mathematical support) and ask students to do both exact and approximate work (exact value then approximate to three decimals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation tasks (judging correctness and interpreting representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Another source of rich test items is situations that ask students to interpret a representation, such as a graph, or results produced by technology or another person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give students sample student work or graphs and ask 'Is the work correct? Explain your reasoning' or interpret why plotted points behave as they do (e.g., spacing of points on falling ball graph). These items assess sense-making and justification skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing problem-solving skills through applied, multi-part tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Because developing problem-solving skills is also a goal in all of our courses, we include test items that help us measure progress to this goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realistic optimization or modeling problems with parts that ask for model formulation, solution method description, and approximation methods (e.g., cost-minimization box problem), and include meta-questions that ask students to reflect on methods they used and where else they'd apply similar calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diverse question types: description, estimation, defense, and consistency checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that require students to describe or explain, estimate answers, defend the reasonableness of results, or check the consistency of representations are used more often now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate items that elicit explanations, reasonableness checks, and cross-representation consistency to provide richer information about student understanding than computational items alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate test format and rationale to students
rubrics_metrics.description: As our tests have changed, we have learned to talk with students about these changes. Before a test students should know that our questions may not look like those in the text and understand why they should be able to apply concepts and do more than mimic examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell students what to expect (novel situations, full range of activities), suggest how to prepare (practice skills with/without technology, analyze examples, reflect on big ideas), and provide post-test opportunities to discuss learning, thought processes, and misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsider grading rubrics (analytic vs holistic) and role of tests in assignment mix
rubrics_metrics.description: We suggest also reconsidering as well the grading rubric for tests. Using an analytic or holistic grading rubric can change the messages sent by even a traditional test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose grading schemes that align with instructional goals (analytic rubrics to reward component skills/understanding; holistic for overall performance), and evaluate whether timed, in-class, individual efforts are necessary or if alternative assessments better serve course objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and use of Interactive Questionnaires (IQs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An IQ is an enhanced interactive quiz (controlled by a computer program) offering various aids and guidance to students who receive it by e-mail. Students take IQs at computer terminals and the IQ automatically returns student-entered data to the instructor for placement in the student’s portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IQs to provide semi-individualized detailed responses, modularize problems into parts, present help screens with measurable penalties, allow retries, and automatically collect and tag responses for portfolio assembly and instructor polling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure IQ help screens with explicit point-costed options and track usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers after help screen menu items inform students of how many points they will lose for using that help option. The IQ tracks student use of help screens, returning that data to the instructor via e-mail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer graduated help options with explicit point costs so students self-evaluate help needs; track which help options are used to diagnose learning gaps and to tailor instructor feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated/semi-automated portfolio creation and polling
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated portfolios track each student’s interactions; polling portfolios collect IQ and other interaction data to give an instantaneous report on how a collection of students answered a specific question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tag each piece of IQ responses for automatic placement into portfolios, enable batched evaluating/commenting on specific pieces, and produce reports across students for targeted instructional feedback; default access to portfolios should remain with instructor unless otherwise chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use IQs to focus on small conceptual problem elements and to simplify grading
rubrics_metrics.description: IQs’ highly modular structure assists this process. Data from an IQ is in pieces. You view pieces extracted from a student’s response(s) with the IQ reader. IQs are much easier to grade than similarly enhanced paper and pencil exams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit IQ modularity to isolate conceptual difficulties, batch-grade identical items across students, and send commented pieces automatically to students to support learning and reduce instructor workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider costs and institutional support when implementing programs
rubrics_metrics.description: A full-fledged REU program like the SMALL Project requires a strong commitment by the department as well as the privilege of an NSF grant or other outside funding and substantial institutional resources. Advising a talk is time consuming—over the course of three or four weeks one can spend eight or ten hours advising a talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh benefits (independent work, research experience, graduate preparation) against faculty time commitments and institutional costs (stipends, housing); ensure adequate resource allocation before implementing such programs.
